reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Typically presents in adolescence or early adulthood with progressive blurring and distortion of vision from irregular astigmatism
Frequent changes of spectacle prescription that fail to give satisfactory vision should raise suspicion of a developing ectasia
Often bilateral but asymmetric, and associated with eye rubbing, atopy, and connective tissue disorders such as Down syndrome
Clinical signs include a cone-shaped protrusion of the cornea, thinning at the apex, Vogt striae, Fleischer ring, and a scissoring reflex on retinoscopy
Munson sign is an angular bulging of the lower lid margin seen on downgaze in advanced disease
Corneal topography and tomography are key to early diagnosis and to monitoring progression

Management is staged: spectacles or soft lenses early, rigid gas-permeable or specialty contact lenses for irregular astigmatism, corneal collagen cross-linking to arrest progression, and keratoplasty for advanced scarring or intolerance to lenses
Acute corneal hydrops causes sudden pain, redness, and reduced vision from a break in Descemet membrane allowing aqueous into the stroma
reference.pathophysiology: Keratoconus is a progressive, non-inflammatory ectasia in which the cornea thins and steepens into a conical shape, producing irregular astigmatism and myopia. The stromal thinning reflects disorganisation of collagen lamellae and altered enzyme activity with increased degradation of the corneal matrix. Mechanical stress from chronic eye rubbing and an association with atopy and certain systemic syndromes are recognised contributors. As the cone advances, the apex scars and Descemet membrane may rupture, precipitating acute hydrops with corneal oedema.
additionalInvestigations: Corneal topography and tomography to map curvature and detect early ectasia
Retinoscopy to detect the scissoring reflex
Serial imaging to assess progression and guide cross-linking decisions
Assessment for associated atopy or connective tissue disorders when indicated
redFlags: Sudden pain, marked visual loss, and corneal oedema suggesting acute hydrops
Rapidly progressive steepening in young patients requiring urgent cross-linking assessment
Corneal scarring or lens intolerance indicating need for keratoplasty referral
reference.prognosis: Progression is most rapid in younger patients and often stabilises with age; timely cross-linking can halt deterioration, and most patients achieve good functional vision with lenses, though a minority need corneal transplantation.
pitfalls: Repeatedly changing spectacle prescriptions instead of recognising an underlying ectasia
Overlooking eye rubbing as a modifiable driver of progression
Delaying cross-linking in demonstrable progression, allowing avoidable visual loss
Mistaking acute hydrops for infective keratitis
management: Corneal collagen cross-linking to halt progression in documented or early progressive ectasia
Rigid gas-permeable or scleral contact lenses, with spectacles in mild cases, to correct irregular astigmatism and optimise vision
Counselling to stop eye rubbing and treatment of associated atopy and ocular allergy to slow progression
Intrastromal corneal ring segments to flatten the cone and improve lens tolerance in selected eyes
Management of acute hydrops with topical hypertonic agents and supportive measures while the corneal oedema resolves
Corneal transplantation by deep anterior lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty for advanced scarring or contact-lens intolerance
Serial corneal topography and tomography to monitor progression and guide the timing of cross-linking
